title: Stakeholder analysis & engagement
blurb: Analyse stakeholders by power, interest and attitude, and explain how that analysis makes engagement effective.
question: A road bypass project affects a county council, a regulator, local residents and a tourist board. The project manager has limited time. How does a stakeholder analysis help decide who to engage, how closely and with what messages?

teach.body: Stakeholders are the individuals or groups who have an interest in, or are affected by, the project. Stakeholder analysis identifies them and assesses their interest, their influence or power, their attitude (support or opposition), and their needs and expectations. In plain English: work out who cares, how much they can affect you, and whether they are for or against, before you decide how to engage them.

teach.caption: Analysis is not a one-off: stakeholders' power, interest and attitude shift as the project moves on.
Also called an influence/interest matrix. The quadrant tells you how much effort to put in.

head: Stakeholder
Power / interest
Attitude
Approach
teach.caption: The residents are opposed, so 'keep informed' should include consultation on their concerns, not just newsletters.
Two stakeholders in the same quadrant may need very different handling if one supports and one opposes.

items: Prioritises effort: spend limited time where power and interest are highest.
Tailors messages and methods to each group's needs and concerns.
Anticipates resistance, so concerns can be addressed early.
Builds support by finding and using champions.
Informs the stakeholder engagement plan and the communication plan.

teach.body: The point of analysis is better engagement: the right people, the right level of involvement, the right message, in the right way. It cannot guarantee everyone will support the project, and it does not remove risk. It is revisited as the project goes on, because a quiet stakeholder can suddenly gain power or interest.

teach.text: Grid trap: HIGH power, LOW interest = keep SATISFIED (not 'keep informed'). LOW power, HIGH interest = keep INFORMED. Also beware 'analysis guarantees support' or 'only internal stakeholders count': both are wrong.

items: Stakeholder analysis identifies stakeholders and assesses interest, power, attitude, needs and expectations.
Power/interest grid: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor.
It supports engagement by prioritising effort, tailoring messages, anticipating resistance and building support.
It informs the engagement and communication plans, and is revisited as positions change.

summary: You can now explain how stakeholder analysis assesses interest, power, attitude and needs, place stakeholders on a power/interest grid, and show how this supports engagement by focusing effort, tailoring messages and anticipating resistance. You can also explain why the analysis is revisited during the project.

A.q: How does stakeholder analysis support effective stakeholder engagement?
options: It guarantees that every stakeholder will support the work
It shows where to focus effort and how to tailor engagement
It removes the need to produce a separate communication plan
It limits engagement to stakeholders inside the organisation
A.why: Analysis prioritises effort by power and interest and lets messages and methods be tailored to each group.

whyNot.0: No analysis can guarantee support; it helps build it.
whyNot.2: Analysis informs the communication plan; it doesn't replace it.
whyNot.3: External stakeholders such as regulators and residents can be critical.

A.q: On a power/interest grid, a stakeholder with HIGH power but LOW interest should usually be:
A.why: High-power, low-interest stakeholders are kept satisfied: meet their needs without overloading them.

whyNot.0: Managing closely is for high power AND high interest.
whyNot.1: Keeping informed is for low power, high interest.
whyNot.3: Monitoring is for low power, low interest.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT normally assessed in a stakeholder analysis?
A.why: Stakeholder analysis looks at interest, influence or power, attitude, needs and expectations, not work package costs.

whyNot.0: Interest is one of the two axes of the grid.
whyNot.1: Power or influence is the other axis of the grid.
whyNot.2: Attitude (support or opposition) is a key part of the analysis.

B.q: A residents' group cares deeply about a new rail depot near their homes but has little formal power over it. Which approach does the analysis suggest?
B.why: Low power, high interest stakeholders are kept informed with regular updates and a chance to be heard.

whyNot.1: Keep satisfied is for high power, low interest.
whyNot.2: Monitoring alone would ignore their high interest.
whyNot.3: Managing closely is for those with high power as well as high interest.

B.q: Which document is most directly shaped by the stakeholder analysis?
B.why: The communication plan (and the stakeholder engagement plan) is based on the stakeholder analysis.

whyNot.0: The CBS breaks down costs, not stakeholder needs.
whyNot.2: The configuration log tracks items and versions.
whyNot.3: The network shows activity dependencies and the critical path.

B.q: Analysis shows a senior director has high power, high interest and is strongly opposed. What should the engagement prioritise?
options: Leaving them off updates to avoid any conflict
Treating them exactly as all other stakeholders
Engaging early to understand and address concerns
Logging them as an issue for the sponsor to solve
B.why: Analysis lets you anticipate resistance: a powerful opponent needs early, active engagement to understand and address their concerns.

whyNot.0: Excluding a powerful stakeholder usually increases resistance.
whyNot.1: Analysis exists precisely so that engagement can be tailored.
whyNot.3: Opposition is not an issue in the APM sense; it is managed through engagement.

C.q: Midway through a project, a regulator that had shown little interest announces a review of the scheme. What should the project manager do?
options: Revisit the analysis and step up engagement with them
Keep the original analysis, as it was agreed at the start
Stop all engagement with the regulator until closure
Pass all contact with the regulator to the project team
C.why: The regulator's interest has risen, so the analysis should be revisited and engagement increased (likely to manage closely).

whyNot.1: Analysis is not fixed; positions change and it must be updated.
whyNot.2: Withdrawing from a powerful, now-interested stakeholder invites trouble.
whyNot.3: Delegating without a plan ignores their new priority; the approach must change first.

C.q: Which THREE of the following are ways that stakeholder analysis supports engagement? 1. Prioritising effort 2. Tailoring messages 3. Guaranteeing support 4. Anticipating resistance
C.why: Analysis helps prioritise effort, tailor messages and anticipate resistance. It cannot guarantee support.

whyNot.1: Guaranteeing support is not possible, and tailoring messages is missing.
whyNot.2: Guaranteeing support is not possible, and prioritising effort is missing.

C.q: Two stakeholders both sit in the 'manage closely' quadrant, but one is a keen supporter and the other is opposed. Why does the analysis record attitude as well?
options: Attitude decides who chairs the project board
Attitude replaces the need for the power axis
The same quadrant can need different handling
Opposed stakeholders are removed from the grid
C.why: Power and interest set the level of engagement; attitude shapes its nature, such as using a supporter as a champion and addressing an opponent's concerns.

whyNot.0: The sponsor normally chairs the board; attitude doesn't decide it.
whyNot.1: Attitude adds to power and interest; it doesn't replace them.
whyNot.3: Opposed stakeholders stay in the analysis: they often need the most care.

reteach.title: Think of organising a music festival
reteach.question: You're organising a weekend music festival in a village field. Who do you need to talk to, and how often?

blocks.h: Not everyone needs the same attention
blocks.body: The licensing council can shut you down, but only cares about safety paperwork: keep them satisfied. The landowner can cancel and cares a lot: manage them closely. Villagers worried about noise can't stop you but care deeply: keep them informed and listen. A nearby town's tourist office barely notices: just monitor. Treat everyone the same and you'll either exhaust yourself or annoy the wrong people.

blocks.text: If the villagers form a protest group and lobby the council, their power rises. Redo the grid: analysis has to keep up with change.

explain.body: A stakeholder is any individual or group with an interest in, or affected by, the project. Identify them widely: internal and external, supporters and opponents, people who can influence the project and people it affects.

test.q: Which best defines a project stakeholder?
options: Anyone with a financial share in the organisation
A member of the project team or the governance board
Anyone with an interest in, or affected by, the project
A person who has formally approved the business case
test.why: A stakeholder is any individual or group with an interest in, or affected by, the project.

whyNot.0: Shareholders may be stakeholders, but the term is much wider.
whyNot.1: Team and board members are stakeholders, but so are users, regulators and the public.
whyNot.3: Approvers are a small subset of stakeholders.

explain.body: For each stakeholder, assess their interest, their power or influence, their attitude (supportive, neutral or opposed), and their needs and expectations.

items.label: how much they can affect it

test.q: Besides power and interest, which factor in the analysis best helps predict resistance?
test.why: Attitude (support or opposition) shows who may resist, so concerns can be addressed early.

whyNot.1: Job title may hint at power, but not whether they support the project.
whyNot.2: Meeting preferences help logistics, not predicting resistance.
whyNot.3: People don't sit on the WBS; it breaks down work.

explain.body: Plot each stakeholder by power and interest. High/high: manage closely. High power, low interest: keep satisfied. Low power, high interest: keep informed. Low/low: monitor.

test.q: On a power/interest grid, which group needs the most active engagement?
test.why: High power, high interest stakeholders are managed closely: they can make or break the project and care about it.

whyNot.0: Low/low stakeholders are monitored with minimal effort.
whyNot.1: These are kept informed rather than managed closely.
whyNot.2: These are kept satisfied, not engaged in detail.

explain.body: The analysis feeds the stakeholder engagement plan and the communication plan: who gets what message, how and how often. It is reviewed as the project progresses.

test.q: Stakeholder analysis feeds most directly into which TWO plans?
options: The risk management and quality plans
The schedule and cost control plans
test.why: Stakeholder analysis informs the stakeholder engagement plan and the communication plan.

whyNot.0: Analysis may raise risks, but it mainly shapes engagement and communication.
whyNot.2: Procurement and resources are not built from stakeholder analysis.
whyNot.3: Schedules and budgets come from the WBS and estimates.
